## The question

Crossing volume drives everything downstream in a border brokerage — staffing,
clearance lead time, where a delay is about to happen. The data is public and
goes back to 1996, which is long enough to separate normal seasonality from an
actual shift.

## The data

::: {.provenance}
<dl>
  <dt>Source</dt>
  <dd>
    <a href="https://www.bts.gov/browse-statistical-products-and-data/border-border-crossingentry-data/border-crossingentry-data">Border
    Crossing/Entry Data</a>, Bureau of Transportation Statistics.
  </dd>
  <dt>Coverage</dt>
  <dd>Monthly counts by port, measure (trucks, loaded containers, personal
  vehicles, pedestrians, rail), 1996–present.</dd>
  <dt>Retrieved</dt><dd>[Date]</dd>
  <dt>Known limits</dt>
  <dd>
    Counts inbound crossings only, not outbound, and counts conveyances rather
    than shipment value. A truck is a truck whether it is full or empty.
  </dd>
</dl>
:::

## Approach

[Replace with what you did:]

- Load to SQLite; the file is long-format and clean enough to query directly.
- Index monthly volumes to a 2019 baseline per port so ports of different sizes
  are comparable.
- Decompose one port series into trend and seasonal components to show the
  size of the normal summer peak against the 2020 break.
- Compare Blaine, Sumas, and Lynden against the northern border as a whole.

```{sql}
#| eval: false
select port_name,
       strftime('%Y', date) as yr,
       sum(value) filter (where measure = 'Trucks') as trucks
from crossings
where border = 'US-Canada Border'
  and state = 'Washington'
group by port_name, yr
order by port_name, yr;
```

## What I would do differently

[Candidates: conveyance counts are a poor proxy for trade value, so joining
Census district-level trade data would show whether fewer trucks carried more
value; and a proper interrupted time series would test the 2020 break rather
